The Black-crested antshrike (Sakesphorus canadensis) is a medium-sized thamnophilid that inhabits dry to moist lowland forests and scrublands across northern South America. Comparing these values to those of sympatric congeners, the clutch size is fairly typical for the genus, aligning with the average for thamnophilids that rely on arthropod prey. The relatively modest number of eggs per effort is balanced by the capacity for a second nesting attempt within the same season, a strategy that appears advantageous in the seasonally variable environments the species occupies. The interval between successive broods is likely constrained by the time required to complete the nesting cycle and the energetic demands of provisioning nestlings, topics that warrant further investigation under controlled conditions.

The loss in mass between the fresh egg and the hatchling is attributable to metabolic water loss and the consumption of yolk reserves during embryonic development, a pattern common among passerine birds. The maximum lifespan of the Black-crested antshrike in the wild, as inferred from banding returns and long-term population studies, appears to be approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] when environmental temperatures average around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is relatively substantial for a bird of its size, suggesting that adult mortality rates are low once individuals have established territories and mastered the foraging techniques required to exploit local insect prey. This delay of roughly one year between hatching and first reproduction is common among thamnophilids and is likely related to the time required to acquire a territory and a mate, as well as to complete skeletal growth. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males sporting a distinctive black crest and chest that contrasts with their white underparts, while females display a more rufous and buff coloration. This plumage difference is thought to play a role in both intra- and intersexual selection during the breeding season. The ecological role of the Black-crested antshrike as an insectivore is also noteworthy; they frequently join mixed-species foraging flocks, gleaning arthropods from foliage and branches in the understory.
